steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the lead section of the encyclopedia article on algorithmic information theory: what it is, its main achievements, and what it studies and why.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Definition: branch of theoretical CS, computation vs. information of computably generated objects; Chaitin's description
- Main achievements
- What AIT studies and its motivations; its three core concepts

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Definition
  - AIT = branch of theoretical computer science
  - relationship between computation and information of computably generated objects (not stochastically generated), e.g. strings, other data structures
  - computational incompressibility "mimics" relations/inequalities of information theory (except a constant depending only on chosen universal programming language)
  - Gregory Chaitin: [quote: Shannon's information theory + Turing's computability theory in a cocktail shaker]
- Main achievements
  - formalizing a universal measure for irreducible information content of computably generated objects
  - algorithmic complexity follows (self-delimited case) the same inequalities as entropy, as in classical information theory (except for a constant)
  - randomness is incompressibility
  - randomly generated software: probability of occurrence of any data structure is of the order of the shortest program generating it on a universal machine
- Scope and motivations
  - studies measures of irreducible information content of strings / other data structures
  - most mathematical objects describable as strings or limits of sequences of strings -> wide variety of objects, incl. integers
  - motivation: information carried by mathematical objects, as in metamathematics (incompleteness results mentioned below)
  - other motivations: limits of classical information theory for single, fixed objects; formalizing randomness; meaningful probabilistic inference without prior knowledge of distribution (i.i.d., Markovian, even stationary?)
  - founded on three concepts + relations: algorithmic complexity, algorithmic randomness, algorithmic probability

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Algorithmic information theory (AIT) is a branch of theoretical computer science. It is concerned with the relationship between computation and information of objects that are computably generated (as opposed to stochastically generated), like strings or any other data structure. Put another way, algorithmic information theory shows that computational incompressibility "mimics" the relations or inequalities that are found in information theory (except for a constant which only depends on the universal programming language that was chosen). Gregory Chaitin describes it as "the result of putting Shannon's information theory and Turing's computability theory into a cocktail shaker and shaking vigorously."

Apart from formalizing a universal measure for the irreducible information content of computably generated objects, AIT had some main achievements. It showed that algorithmic complexity actually follows the same inequalities that entropy does (in the self-delimited case, and except for a constant), as in classical information theory. It showed that randomness is incompressibility. And it showed that, within the realm of randomly generated software, the probability that any data structure occurs is of the order of the shortest program that generates it when it runs on a universal machine.

- Scope and motivations
  - studies measures of irreducible information content of strings / other data structures
  - most mathematical objects describable as strings or limits of sequences of strings -> wide variety of objects, incl. integers
  - motivation: information carried by mathematical objects, as in metamathematics (incompleteness results mentioned below)
  - other motivations: limits of classical information theory for single, fixed objects; formalizing randomness; meaningful probabilistic inference without prior knowledge of distribution (i.i.d., Markovian, even stationary?)
  - founded on three concepts + relations: algorithmic complexity, algorithmic randomness, algorithmic probability

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Algorithmic information theory (AIT) is a branch of theoretical computer science. It is concerned with the relationship between computation and information of objects that are computably generated (as opposed to stochastically generated), like strings or any other data structure. Put another way, algorithmic information theory shows that computational incompressibility "mimics" the relations or inequalities that are found in information theory (except for a constant which only depends on the universal programming language that was chosen). Gregory Chaitin describes it as "the result of putting Shannon's information theory and Turing's computability theory into a cocktail shaker and shaking vigorously."

Apart from formalizing a universal measure for the irreducible information content of computably generated objects, AIT had some main achievements. It showed that algorithmic complexity actually follows the same inequalities that entropy does (in the self-delimited case, and except for a constant), as in classical information theory. It showed that randomness is incompressibility. And it showed that, within the realm of randomly generated software, the probability that any data structure occurs is of the order of the shortest program that generates it when it runs on a universal machine.

AIT mainly studies measures of the irreducible information content of strings (or other data structures). Most mathematical objects can be described in terms of strings, or as the limit of a sequence of strings, so it can be used to study a wide variety of mathematical objects, integers included. One of the main motivations of AIT is studying the information carried by mathematical objects, as in the field of metamathematics, e.g., as the incompleteness results mentioned below show. Other main motivations were getting past the limitations of classical information theory for single and fixed objects, formalizing the concept of randomness, and finding a meaningful probabilistic inference without knowing the probability distribution beforehand (e.g., whether it is independent and identically distributed, Markovian, or even stationary). So AIT is basically founded on three main mathematical concepts and the relations between them: algorithmic complexity, algorithmic randomness, and algorithmic probability.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Algorithmic information theory (AIT) is a branch of theoretical computer science that concerns itself with the relationship between computation and information of computably generated objects (as opposed to stochastically generated), such as strings or any other data structure. In other words, algorithmic information theory shows that computational incompressibility "mimics" (except for a constant that depends only on the chosen universal programming language) the relations or inequalities found in information theory. According to Gregory Chaitin, it is "the result of putting Shannon's information theory and Turing's computability theory into a cocktail shaker and shaking vigorously."[1]

Besides formalizing a universal measure for the irreducible information content of computably generated objects, some main achievements of AIT were to show that: algorithmic complexity in fact follows (in the self-delimited case) the same inequalities (except for a constant[2]) as entropy does in classical information theory; randomness is incompressibility; and, within the realm of randomly generated software, the probability of occurrence of any data structure is of the order of the shortest program that generates it when running on a universal machine.[3]

AIT principally studies measures of the irreducible information content of strings (or other data structures). Because most mathematical objects can be described in terms of strings, or as the limit of a sequence of strings, it can be used to study a wide variety of mathematical objects, including integers. One of the main motivations behind AIT is the study of the information carried by mathematical objects, as in the field of metamathematics, e.g., as shown by the incompleteness results mentioned below. Other main motivations came from overcoming the limitations of classical information theory for single and fixed objects, formalizing the concept of randomness, and finding a meaningful probabilistic inference without prior knowledge of the probability distribution (e.g., whether it is independent and identically distributed, Markovian, or even stationary). In this way, AIT is basically founded upon three main mathematical concepts and the relations between them: algorithmic complexity, algorithmic randomness, and algorithmic probability.

References:
[1] Algorithmic Information Theory. http://www.cs.auckland.ac.nz/research/groups/CDMTCS/docs/ait.php
[2] or, for the mutual algorithmic information, informing the algorithmic complexity of the input along with the input itself.
[3] Downey, Rodney G.. (2010). Algorithmic Randomness and Complexity. Springer. https://books.google.com/books?id=FwIKhn4RYzYC
